As a comparison, let's look at SELinux. It has two modes: Permissive and Enforcing. When in Permissive mode, SELinux only monitors the OS and never acts based on the rules in its configuration. On the other hand, Enforcing permits it to act accordingly and prevent certain actions from taking place. Invites by itself is essentially SELinux in Permissive mode. It allows for any preexisting user to invite a non-existing user and no action is taken. SAR would be as if the switch was flipped and Voat started only allowing specific accounts to send invites based on a set of criteria. Both features allow for community growth, and you're right that SAR is just an extension of Invites, but just as Enforcing mode is a specific feature of SELinux, SAR would be of Invites, an extension or evolution of its capability.

Every account-based site has the ability to invite users, but not every one of those has the ability to grow during a time of restricted access.
